title: What C++ Is and How a Program Runs

scenes.say: This line is fine in C, and fails in C plus plus. Why? By the end, you'll explain it, and answer all eight core questions out loud.

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Trace a source file all the way to a running process. Follow one variable by value, by reference, and by pointer. And answer the keyword questions: static, const, and struct.

scenes.title: C or C++: what changed?
scenes.statement: C++ began as 'C with classes', and most C programs still compile as C++. So what does C++ actually add?

example.input: The same tiny job, in C and in C++

scenes.say: In nineteen seventy nine, Bjarne Stroustrup added classes to C. Take one tiny job, written in both languages. The question: what does C plus plus add, in one sentence?

cues.output: what does C plus plus add

scenes.head: Same job, two languages
scenes.say: Same job, twice. In C, you call malloc, and you must remember free. Forget it, and memory leaks. In C plus plus, a vector frees its own memory at the closing brace. That's R A I I: the object cleans up after itself. And the speed stays: zero overhead means you don't pay for features you don't use.

panels.label: C
C++
panels.code:
std::vector<int> d(10);
d[0] = 42;

scenes.head: Four things C does not have
scenes.say: Four features C lacks. A namespace groups names so they don't collide. Two functions share the name area, and C plus plus picks by argument type: overloading. A template writes biggest once, for any type. And a reference lets twice change n directly.

scenes.head: C versus C++
scenes.say: Style: C is procedural. C plus plus adds classes and generics. Memory: malloc and free, against R A I I, where smart pointers free themselves. Generic code: macros, against templates. Library: small, against the S T L, with containers and algorithms.
Your turn. This line is fine in C. Malloc returns a void pointer, and C converts it silently. Now compile it as C plus plus. What happens? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `int* p = malloc(sizeof(int));` compiled as C++: what happens?

scenes.head: Why C++ is not a perfect superset
scenes.say: Error. C plus plus won't convert a void pointer to an int pointer silently, so add a cast. And class is a keyword in C plus plus, so rename that variable. So C plus plus is almost a superset of C. In one sentence: C plus plus is C, plus R A I I, templates, and the S T L, at zero overhead.

panels.label: C only
C++

scenes.title: What does g++ main.cpp do?
scenes.statement: One command turns main.cpp into a program. Name the tools it runs, in order, and which one reports which kind of error.
scenes.say: One command looks like one step. Start with main dot c p p, and finish with a dot out. Which tools run in between, and in what order?

scenes.head: Four tools, in order
scenes.say: Four tools run in order. First the preprocessor pastes in every include and expands macros. Then the compiler checks syntax and types, and translates C plus plus into assembly. The assembler turns that into machine code. Finally the linker joins object files and libraries into one program.

scenes.head: Stop at any stage yourself
scenes.say: Here is main dot c p p. An include, a macro, and main. Now stop after each stage. Dash E stops after the preprocessor. Dash S stops after the compiler. Dash c stops after the assembler, and leaves main dot o. With no flag, the linker runs. Run it.

panels.code:
g++ -E main.cpp -o main.i
g++ -S main.cpp -o main.s
g++ -c main.cpp -o main.o
g++ main.o -o a.out
./a.out

scenes.say: Your turn. A file declares a function add, calls it, but never writes its body. Which tool complains? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `add` is declared but never defined. Which tool reports an error?

scenes.head: Why the stages matter: errors
scenes.say: The linker. The compiler is happy: it only needs to know add exists. But the linker can't find its body anywhere, so it fails with undefined reference. L D is the linker.

output.text:
main.cpp:(.text+0xf): undefined reference to `add(int, int)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

scenes.head: Run: the OS takes over
scenes.say: When you run it, the operating system's loader creates a process. Machine code goes in the text part. Globals go in the data part. Then it adds a heap and a stack. Startup code runs, then main. When main returns zero, that is the exit code, and zero means success.

scenes.title: Declared or defined?
scenes.statement: Two lines can look alike: one only names a variable, the other creates it. Which is which, and why does the difference decide linker errors?

example.input: extern int g;   vs   int g = 3;
example.output: a name only   vs   memory reserved

scenes.say: Two lines look almost alike. Mix them up, and the linker rejects your build. Here they are: extern int g, and int g equals three. Which only names, and which creates?

scenes.head: A sign and a building
scenes.say: Think of a street sign. The sign says there's a bakery. The building is the bakery. Sign: declaration. Building: definition.

scenes.head: Three declarations, three definitions
scenes.say: Three declarations: a variable, a function, a struct. Each only names a thing, saying it exists. Now the definitions. The variable gets memory. The function gets its body. The struct gets its full layout. Every definition is also a declaration, but not the other way around.

scenes.head: This is why headers exist
scenes.say: The header holds only the declaration, so any file can include it. Main dot c p p includes it and calls add. Exactly one source file holds the definition. The compiler checks each file alone. Then the linker connects every call to the single definition.
Your turn. Two source files each define int counter equals zero. Each compiles alone. What happens when you build them together? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: a.cpp and b.cpp both define `int counter = 0;`. Build both: what happens?

scenes.head: The one definition rule
scenes.say: The linker. Each file compiles alone, so the compiler is fine. But the linker finds two definitions of counter. The fix: extern in a header, one definition. Declare often, define once.

panels.code: int counter = 0;

panels.label: 2nd definition
panels.code:
int counter = 0;
int main() {}

panels.label: the fix
panels.code: extern int counter;

output.cmd: g++ a.cpp b.cpp 2>&1 | grep -o "multiple definition of .counter."

scenes.title: Add one to n
scenes.statement: A function adds one to n, which is 5. What does the function receive: a copy, an alias, or an address? And does the caller see the change?
scenes.say: A function adds one to a variable. Our variable n equals five. Three ways to hand it over. Which ones let the function change n?

scenes.head: 1 · By value: a copy
scenes.say: Think of a document. By value hands over a photocopy. Calling addOne makes x, a brand new copy of n. Add one to the copy: six. The function returns, the copy vanishes, and n is still five.

scenes.head: 2 · By reference: an alias
scenes.say: By reference. The ampersand means x is not a copy. It's a second name on the same document. Add one through x, and n itself becomes six. Nothing was copied. Print n, and it shows six.

scenes.head: 3 · By pointer: a copy of the address
scenes.say: By pointer. x holds a copy of n's address, a note saying where n lives. Star x follows the note to the real n, and adds one. The caller wrote ampersand n, so it's obvious n may change. But x could be null, so check it first.

notes.text: x may be null: check it

scenes.say: Your turn. Same pointer, new rule: multiply the value by three, not add one. Start with n equal to five. What is n afterwards? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Same pointer, but `*x = *x * 3` with n = 5. What is n afterwards?

scenes.head: Same pointer, times three
scenes.say: Fifteen. Star x follows the note to n, and multiplies its value by three. The note never changes. Only the value at its target does.

scenes.head: One assignment tells them apart
scenes.say: Now pointer against reference. Both start at a. The pointer p stores a's address. The reference r is not a separate variable. It's another name for a. Point p at b, and p moves. But r equals b copies twenty into a, because r is a, forever. Print them: twenty, twenty, twenty.

scenes.head: More rules for each
scenes.say: More rules. A pointer can be null. A reference must be bound when it's created, so this line fails with a real compiler error. A reference is never null. Pointers also support arithmetic: it plus plus walks to the next element. References don't.

output.text: rules.cpp:3:10: error: ‘r’ declared as reference but not initialized

scenes.head: Value, reference, pointer
scenes.say: The call: only the pointer needs an ampersand. What is copied: the object, nothing, an address. Can it change n? Not by value. Can it be null? Only a pointer. Use value for small types, const T reference for big objects, pointers when optional.

scenes.title: Where does `a` live?
scenes.statement: A function declares `int a = 5` and calls `new int(42)`. Which one lives on the stack, which on the heap, and what happens when the function returns?

example.output: a, p on the stack; 42 on the heap

scenes.say: Two places hold your data. Take a function with a local a, and a new int. Who lives where, and when does each one disappear?

scenes.head: Plates and a warehouse
scenes.say: Think of two storage spaces. The stack is a pile of plates. Newest goes on top, and it's cleared automatically. The heap is a warehouse. You ask for space, and you must give it back.

scenes.head: Watch memory while f() runs
scenes.say: Call f, and the stack grows a frame on top of main. Local a lives right there. New int asks the heap for room, and the heap hands back an address. The pointer p, on the stack, stores it. Delete gives the room back. When f returns, its frame vanishes, a and p included.

scenes.head: Stack versus heap
scenes.say: Who manages it? The compiler, against you or a smart pointer. Lifetime: until the scope ends, against until freed. Speed: the stack moves one pointer. Size: a few megabytes, against most of the R A M. Typical bugs: overflow, against leaks and dangling pointers.
Your turn. A function declares a local array of ten million ints. That's about forty megabytes. What usually happens when it runs? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: A local `int big[10000000];` is about 40 MB. What usually happens?

scenes.head: Size matters
scenes.say: A stack overflow: it usually crashes, since the stack is small, often one to eight megabytes. A vector fixes it. The vector object sits on the stack, but its ten million elements live on the heap, and it frees them itself. Prefer the stack, and reach the heap through vector, not raw new.

panels.label: fine

scenes.title: Three keywords, three questions
scenes.statement: static, const and constexpr look related. What does each one actually promise?

example.output: lifetime · can it change · compile time

scenes.say: Three keywords look related, and people mix them up. Here they are, side by side. What does each one promise?

scenes.head: One question each
scenes.say: Each keyword answers a different question. static: how long does it live? const: can it change after it's set? constexpr: can the compiler know it before the program runs?

scenes.head: static: how long it lives
scenes.say: First, static as lifetime. A static local is initialized once, and keeps its value between calls. Call counter twice. Then print the third call. It prints three, not one.

scenes.head: static: who can see it
scenes.say: Second, static as visibility. At file level, static hides a function from other files. Inside a class, a static member belongs to the class, not to any object. There is one shared count, so three players make it three.
Your turn. A variable n is read from the keyboard, at run time. Which line fails to compile: the const one, or the constexpr one? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: n is read from cin. Which line fails to compile?

scenes.head: const and constexpr
scenes.say: The constexpr line. Const only means read only, so size, computed from n at run time, is fine. Constexpr needs the value at compile time. Four times four is sixteen, so sq works, and can size an array. But n comes from the keyboard, so the last line fails.

output.text: the value of ‘n’ is not usable in a constant expression

scenes.head: Three keywords, side by side
scenes.say: Static: how long does it live, and who sees it? Its value can still change. Const: can it change? Set once, maybe at run time. Constexpr: known at compile time? Fixed by the compiler, and every constexpr is also const.
rows: set once, maybe at run time

scenes.title: struct or class?
scenes.statement: Both can have constructors, methods and inheritance. So what is the difference, and which one do you pick?

example.input: struct A { int x; };  class B { int x; };
example.output: A::x is public, B::x is private

scenes.say: The answer is short, but it's a common trap. Two types, one member each. What is the difference, and which one do you pick?

scenes.head: The only difference: default access
scenes.say: Think of an open drawer and a locked one. A struct is the open drawer: members are public by default. A class is the locked one: private by default. That's the whole difference. Set x on the struct: fine. Set x on the class: error.

output.text: access.cpp:6:13: error: ‘int B::x’ is private within this context

scenes.say: Your turn. Base has a public member v. Class D inherits from Base, and says nothing about access. Can main set v on a D? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `class D : Base {};` Base::v is public. Does `d.v = 1;` compile?

scenes.head: The same default for inheritance
scenes.say: No. A class inherits privately by default, so Base's public v becomes private inside D. A struct inherits publicly by default. Write public or private yourself, and the two keywords are interchangeable.

output.text: inherit.cpp:8:16: error: ‘int Base::v’ is inaccessible within this context

scenes.head: So which do you pick?
scenes.say: An invariant is a rule the object must always keep. By convention, struct for plain data with no rules, like a point. Class when there's an invariant to protect. Here, balance is private, so the only way to change it is deposit, which refuses negative amounts.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: C versus C plus plus? Procedural, against classes, templates, R A I I. The cost? Zero overhead. A strict superset? Almost: malloc needs a cast.
rows: C: procedural, manual memory. C++: classes, RAII, templates, STL
Zero overhead: you pay for what you use

scenes.head: Compile and run, in order
scenes.say: What happens when you compile and run? Four tools: preprocess, compile, assemble, link. Compiler reports types. Linker reports undefined references. The O S loads it.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Declaration versus definition? Names it, or creates it. How often? Declare many times, define once. Define twice? The linker reports multiple definition.
rows: Name and type vs memory, body, layout

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Stack versus heap? Stack: automatic, fast, small. Heap: yours, large. Lifetime? Scope end, against until freed. A huge local array? Stack overflow, so use a vector.
rows: Stack: automatic, fast, small. Heap: yours, large

scenes.head: Static, const, constexpr
scenes.say: What does static mean? Lifetime and visibility, not constness. Const? Read only once set, maybe at run time. Constexpr? Known at compile time, and it implies const.

scenes.head: Value, reference, pointer
scenes.say: By value? A copy, so the caller is unchanged. By reference? An alias, no copy, and the caller sees changes. By pointer? A copy of an address, which can be null, so check it. Big read only objects? Const reference.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Pointer versus reference? An object holding an address, or an alias. Null or re-point? Pointers can, references never. Which by default? Reference. Pointer for nothing, or re-pointing.
rows: Object holding an address vs an alias
Reference; pointer for nothing or re-pointing

scenes.say: Your turn, a self-test. Box is a struct, Tag is a class, and each has one int v. Which assignment fails to compile? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Box is a struct with one int v. Tag is a class with one int v. Which assignment fails?

scenes.head: Struct versus class, in one run
scenes.say: The Tag line fails. Box is a struct, so v is public. Tag is a class, so v is private. Struct versus class: only default access. Inheritance: same rule, struct public, class private. Struct for plain data, class for invariants.
